description: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
name: TokenEconomizer
readme_text:
# TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents

Aaron J. Li1, Weijia Xu2, Chandan Singh2, Zixiao Chen3, Jeevana Priya Inala2, Charlotte Siska3,
Acar Tamersoy3, Bin Yu1, Ion Stoica1, Michel Galley2, Jianfeng Gao2

1UC Berkeley   2Microsoft Research   3Microsoft Security

Our measurement on SWE-Bench tasks: 18.4–30.9% lower mean cost across five agent–model combinations, cheaper in all 30 repository × combination cells, and Pass@1 up in 4 of 5. Results

TokenEconomizer makes coding agents cheaper to run in the repositories you work in often, without changing the agent itself. It learns from the sessions an agent has already run in a repository, and uses that experience to cut waste in the sessions that follow. It has three mechanisms: - **Micro-skills: remember how the repository works.** Sessions keep rediscovering the same facts: a build step that must run first, the spelling of a command that works here (`python -m pytest` where `pytest` is missing, `npx tsc` where `tsc` is), an environment variable a command needs, where generated files live. Micro-skills learns such facts, in any language, from two sources: failures that repeat across sessions, and a model that reviews the recent sessions every *k* sessions (*k* = 3) and proposes facts. A fact is stated at the start of each session once three sessions have confirmed it, and dropped when later sessions contradict it. - **Tool pruning: stop loading tools that go unused.** Every loaded tool's definition is sent with every request. A tool that goes unused over *p* prompts spread across at least *m* sessions, or over *s* sessions of any length (*p* = 10, *m* = 2, *s* = 5), is left out of the next sessions through the agent's own settings. One command brings it back. - **Failure-loop intervention (the loop guard): step in when a turn is stuck.** When a turn (the agent's work on one prompt) keeps hitting the same failures, a judge model checks whether it is stuck. If the judge is at least *c* sure (*c* = 0.7), the agent gets a redirect (a short note, added to its context, to try another approach), at most *r* times per turn (*r* = 1). If the turn is still stuck after that, TokenEconomizer tells you how to stop it; it never stops a turn itself. TokenEconomizer is a plugin for **Claude Code**, **Codex**, the **GitHub Copilot CLI** and **Pi**, with experimental support for **opencode**, **Cursor Agent**, **Grok Build**, **Hermes Agent** and the **Antigravity CLI**. Each italic letter above is a setting, shown with its default ([Settings](#settings)), and each mechanism can be turned on or off. The plugin announces each action in one line, and if any part of it fails, your session carries on as if it were not installed. Its model calls (the fact proposer, and the judge with the redirect it writes) run through your own agent, on the same plan or login, and their cost is included in its reports. What it learns stays on your machine, in `~/.tokeneconomizer`. ## Results The paper ran five agent–model combinations on the same 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories. Each task ran as its own session, and each repository's tasks ran in order, starting with nothing learned. Costs include every model call TokenEconomizer made. Within each repository and combination, cost fell by 5–40%. The savings held on Web-Bench (16–21% lower) and on two security-auditing benchmarks where every task is in a new repository (6–20% lower). The [project page](https://tokeneconomizer.github.io) has interactive charts, per-repository numbers and nine annotated runs, and [`experiments/`](experiments/README.md) reruns the SWE-Bench and Web-Bench experiments. ## How it works

Coding agents are built to finish tasks, not to keep them cheap. Every turn pays again for the agent's instructions, every loaded tool, and the conversation so far. Developers use the same agent on the same repository again and again, so much of that cost repeats: the same facts rediscovered, the same unused tools sent, the same kinds of failing loops. TokenEconomizer leaves the agent's model, weights and code alone and learns across a repository's sessions instead of treating each one on its own, so whatever the plugin spends is paid back over the sessions that follow. Four principles guide the mechanisms: - **Work through what the agent already reads.** Facts enter the context at session start, and tools are removed through the agent's own settings, so nothing depends on the agent learning a new tool. - **Count cost as it is billed.** Most tokens in a session are cached re-reads, so cost is computed with cache pricing, and it includes the plugin's own model calls. - **Protect task success.** Facts form only from repeated evidence, tools are removed only after going unused, and the loop guard leaves alone a turn that is still making progress. - **Keep every action reversible.** A fact that later sessions contradict is dropped, removed tools can be given back, and the loop guard only redirects and tells you: stopping a turn is your call. ## Quick start You need one of these agents, signed in any way it supports, and Python 3.10 or newer on `PATH`. The plugin needs no API key of its own and never handles credentials, so any plan or login works. ### Install Run these commands in the folder where you want to keep the clone. Claude Code, Codex, the Copilot CLI and opencode run the plugin from the clone, so leave it in place. Then start the agent in one of your repositories. **Claude Code** ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git claude plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer" claude plugin install tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer ``` Start `claude`, trust the folder (**Yes, I trust this folder**), and run `/tokeneconomizer:status`, allowing its script if asked. Once per machine, and again after Claude Code updates, run `/tokeneconomizer:toolprune refresh-catalog`. **Codex** ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git codex plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer" codex plugin add tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer ``` Start `codex`, choose **Trust and continue** for the folder, then at **Hooks need review** choose **Trust all and continue**. The hooks take effect from your next Codex session, so quit (`/exit`), start `codex` again, and check with `$tokeneconomizer:status`. **Copilot CLI** ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git copilot plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer" copilot plugin install tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer ``` Start `copilot`, choose **Yes, and remember this folder for future sessions**, and run `/tokeneconomizer:status`, choosing **Yes** to run its script. Once per machine, and again after Copilot updates, run `/tokeneconomizer:toolprune refresh-catalog`. **Pi** ```sh pi install git:github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer ``` Start `pi` and run `/te status`. **Cursor Agent** (experimental) ```sh python scripts/build_plugin.py --out ~/.cursor/plugins/local/ ``` Reload Cursor, confirm `tokeneconomizer` appears in Customize, then send a prompt in a repository. Check its state from a terminal with `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host cursor status`. Cursor's published hooks provide session, prompt, tool-result and completion events. Its transcript format and per-session token usage are not a supported public interface, so the adapter records needed hook events locally and reports session cost as unavailable. Cursor support is macOS and Linux only: on Windows, Cursor runs hook commands through PowerShell, and this plugin's launcher is a POSIX shell script. **Grok Build** (experimental) ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git grok plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer" grok plugin install tokeneconomizer --trust ``` Grok runs Claude Code plugins, so this is the Claude Code plugin: grok loads `plugin/hooks/hooks.json` and TokenEconomizer recognises the grok session in the hook payload. (If you already installed it for Claude Code, grok reads `~/.claude/plugins` and runs it in your sessions; this version reads those as grok sessions.) Micro-skills and the loop guard only; tool pruning is not available. Confirm `tokeneconomizer` is enabled in `grok plugin list`, start `grok`, and check with `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host grok status`. The learned facts arrive with the session's first tool call, not at its start ([its limits](plugin/README.md#grok-build)). **Antigravity CLI** (`agy`; experimental; micro-skills' LLM-free facts only) ```sh python scripts/build_plugin.py --out dist/marketplace agy plugin install dist/marketplace/tokeneconomizer ``` Start `agy` and send a prompt in a repository, then check with `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host antigravity status`. `agy` has no plugin commands, so the plugin's commands run from a terminal. The plugin makes no model call through `agy`, which has no option that runs a prompt with every tool off, so the paid proposer and the loop guard are off and tool pruning is not available. macOS and Linux only: on Windows `agy` runs hook commands through `cmd /c`, and this plugin's launcher is a POSIX shell script. See [its limits](plugin/README.md#antigravity-cli). **opencode** (experimental) ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode/plugins ln -s "$PWD/TokenEconomizer/plugin/opencode/tokeneconomizer.ts" ~/.config/opencode/plugins/ ``` The one file serves both generations: opencode 1.x reads its `server` entry, 2.x its `setup`. Start `opencode` and send a prompt, then check in the repository with `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host opencode status`. opencode has no plugin commands, so the plugin's commands run from a terminal. **Hermes Agent** (experimental; micro-skills and the loop guard, on the classic CLI and one-shot runs) ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git ln -s "$PWD/TokenEconomizer/plugin/hermes" ~/.hermes/plugins/tokeneconomizer hermes plugins enable tokeneconomizer hermes gateway restart ``` Link it rather than running `hermes plugins install`, which leaves the launchers behind when given this directory and refuses the whole repository at its security scan. Send a prompt, then check in the repository with `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host hermes status`. If the install worked, the status command prints a short status block. `refresh-catalog` records every tool a session loads (without a model call), so that tool pruning can consider all of them. Keep the marketplace path absolute, as above: the Copilot CLI reads a relative path such as `./TokenEconomizer` as the name of a GitHub repository. To update: | Agent | Update | |---|---| | Claude Code, Copilot CLI, opencode | `git pull` in the clone | | Hermes Agent | `git pull` in the clone, then `hermes gateway restart` | | Antigravity CLI | build the bundle again and `agy plugin install` it | | Codex | `git pull` in the clone, then the `codex plugin add` line again | | Pi | `pi update --extensions` | **[`plugin/README.md`](plugin/README.md)** walks through each agent in more detail, including uninstalling, using Copilot with your own model key, and troubleshooting. ### Supported versions | Agent | Supported | Older versions | |---|---|---| | Claude Code | 2.1.300 to 2.1.310 | not supported | | Codex | 0.153.1 to 0.164.0 | not supported | | Copilot CLI | 1.0.83 to 1.0.102 | not supported | | Pi | 1.2.0 to 1.3.0 | 0.99.x: load the extension by path (below) | | Cursor Agent (experimental) | 3.24.9 and cursor-agent 2026.11.05, macOS and Linux (below) | not tested | | Grok Build (experimental) | 1.0.70 | not tested | | opencode (experimental) | 1.19.5 and 2.2.0 | not tested | | Hermes Agent (experimental) | 0.22.5 | not tested | | Antigravity CLI (experimental) | agy 1.5.1, macOS and Linux | not tested | The commands above were tested on the oldest and newest version in each range; newer versions have not been tested yet. - **Codex before 0.141.0** does not run plugin hooks at all. - **Pi 0.99.x**: instead of `pi install`, clone the repository and start each session with `pi --extension /path/to/TokenEconomizer/plugin/pi/tokeneconomizer.ts`, using your clone's full path; `git pull` in the clone updates it. - **opencode** support is experimental: it was tested on 1.19.5 and 2.2.0 only, and not in the 2.x terminal UI. - **Cursor Agent** support is experimental. Cursor 3.24.9 loaded the local plugin. On `cursor-agent` 2026.11.05, `cursor-agent --trust -p` delivered `sessionStart`, `postToolUse`, `afterShellExecution` and `sessionEnd`, but not `beforeSubmitPrompt` or `stop`; context returned from `sessionStart` and `postToolUse` reached the model. Prompts are then counted from Cursor's own transcript and a run that ends as completed closes its turn. Session usage stays unavailable, and the interactive TUI has not been tested. - **Grok Build** support is experimental: it was verified on 1.0.70 only, against its documented hook contract and live hook payloads. Learned facts reach the model with the session's first tool call, and tool pruning is not available. See [its limits](plugin/README.md#grok-build). - **Antigravity CLI** support is experimental: it was written against agy 1.5.1's hook contract and transcript format, which are not a public interface, and only micro-skills' LLM-free facts are supported: the plugin makes no model call through `agy`. See [its limits](plugin/README.md#antigravity-cli). - **Hermes Agent** support is experimental: it was tested on 0.22.5 only, with a scripted local model and one free real model, on the classic CLI and one-shot runs only. Micro-skills and a redirect reaching a real model are verified there; the still-stuck notice reaching a person is not. Its other surfaces (the Ink TUI, the Desktop app, messaging platforms, cron) and subagents are ignored, and tool pruning is not available. See [its limits](plugin/README.md#hermes-agent). ### Everyday commands Work as usual; the plugin needs nothing from you. To see or change what it does, use its commands. They have the same names on every agent; only the way you type them differs: | Agent | Type a command as | |---|---| | Claude Code, Copilot CLI | `/tokeneconomizer:` | | Codex | `$tokeneconomizer:` | | Pi | `/te ` | | opencode | from a terminal: `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host opencode ` | | Cursor Agent | from a terminal: `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host cursor ` | | Grok Build | from a terminal: `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host grok ` | | Hermes Agent | from a terminal: `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host hermes ` | | Antigravity CLI | from a terminal: `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te --host antigravity ` | | a terminal, in the repository | `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te ` | | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `status` | what it learned and did here, and what your sessions cost | | `microskills` | the facts it injects, and those still forming | | `toolprune` | the tools it left out, and the evidence (not on Pi, opencode, Hermes Agent or the Antigravity CLI) | | `toolprune restore` | give them back; they will not be removed again | | `config` | every setting in effect | | `config set microskills=on` | turn a mechanism on (or `=off`) in this repository; add `--global` for every repository | Inside an agent, a command costs one model turn; from a terminal it is free. The other commands (`repos`, `doctor`, `config unset`, ...) and each agent's permission prompts are listed under [Commands](plugin/README.md#commands). ## Settings Tool pruning and the loop guard are on by default; with these defaults, the plugin calls a model only when a turn shows signs of looping: the judge, and the redirect it writes if it finds the turn stuck. Micro-skills is off by default, because its proposer adds model calls and how much it saves depends on the repository and the work you do there. What each of these calls reads, how often it runs and which model it uses are listed under [Model calls](plugin/README.md#model-calls-and-api-keys). Each mechanism has its own switch (`microskills`, `toolprune`, `loopguard`) that takes `on` or `off`, and the italic letters above are these settings: | | Setting | Default | What it sets | |---|---|---|---| | *k* | `microskills_propose_every` | 3 | sessions between runs of micro-skills' fact proposer | | *p* | `toolprune_evidence` | 10 | prompts a tool must go unused before it is left out | | *m* | `toolprune_min_sessions` | 2 | sessions those prompts must span | | *s* | `toolprune_sessions` | 5 | or this many sessions, of any length | | *q* | `toolprune_quiet_minutes` | 60 | minutes your sessions here must be idle before a deny list is written | | *e* | `loopguard.envelope_min_samples` | 5 | turns here that ended well (no failing check after the last edit) before the loop guard acts | | *c* | `loopguard.judge_confidence` | 0.7 | how sure the judge must be that a turn is stuck | | *r* | `loopguard_nudges` | 1 | redirects per turn before the guard only tells you | | *b* | `loopguard.backstop_mult` | 2.5 | how many times its usual length a churning turn may run before it is redirected without the judge | Change them with `config set`, shown here in Claude Code's form (other agents type it as in [Everyday commands](#everyday-commands)): ```text /tokeneconomizer:config set microskills=on # turn micro-skills on /tokeneconomizer:config set microskills_propose_every=5 # k = 5: propose facts less often /tokeneconomizer:config set toolprune_evidence=20 # p = 20: wait for twenty unused prompts /tokeneconomizer:config set loopguard_nudges=2 # r = 2: redirect twice before telling you ``` Tool pruning counts prompts so that long sessions weigh more, and requires *m* sessions so that a single session never decides alone. It writes the deny list only once your sessions in the repository have been idle for *q* minutes (or, at the latest, a day after the list formed): a conversation resumed after its tools change must write its whole history to the prompt cache again instead of reading it, and after an idle hour that cache has expired anyway. On Claude Code, the plugin can also learn from a repository's earlier sessions, read from Claude Code's own logs oldest first and without any model call. This is off by default, and a repository's history is read only before the plugin has learned from any session there, so turn it on right after installing: with `config set history_import=on --global`, the first session in each repository reads that repository's earlier sessions in the background (see [Earlier sessions](plugin/README.md#earlier-sessions)). A deny list that rests on those earlier sessions waits for `toolprune apply`, even under `auto`. Besides `on` and `off`, two modes are useful: `toolprune=propose` only proposes the deny list, and nothing changes until you run `toolprune apply`; `microskills=envfacts` learns facts only from repeated failures, with no model calls. To change a single session, set an environment variable when you start the agent: `TE_DISABLE=1 claude` turns the whole plugin off, and `TE_LOOPGUARD=off codex` turns off one mechanism (likewise `TE_MICROSKILLS` and `TE_TOOLPRUNE`). Every setting and its default are listed under [Settings](plugin/README.md#settings); each one's environment variable is `TE_` plus its name in capitals. ## What it does on each agent Micro-skills and the loop guard work the same way on every agent. Each agent learns on its own: facts, tool evidence and the loop guard's sense of a usual turn are kept per agent and repository, while settings are shared. Tool pruning acts through each agent's own settings, so what it can leave out differs: | Agent | Tool pruning leaves out | Written to | |---|---|---| | Claude Code | single tools | `.claude/settings.local.json` | | Codex | capability packages | `.codex/config.toml` | | Copilot CLI | whole MCP servers | `.github/copilot/settings.local.json` | | Pi | nothing (Pi loads only four tools) | — | | Cursor Agent | nothing yet | — | | Grok Build | nothing yet | — | | opencode | nothing yet | — | | Hermes Agent | nothing yet | — | | Antigravity CLI | nothing yet | — | Tool pruning adds only its own entries and never touches deny rules you wrote; a settings file it creates is kept out of git (`.git/info/exclude`). On Claude Code, the session-start line that says what it left out shows only in the detailed transcript (**Ctrl+O**), so check with `/tokeneconomizer:toolprune`. `toolprune restore` removes the plugin's entries and nothing else, and tools you give back are not removed again. If the plugin cannot edit a file safely (a `.codex/config.toml` your repository commits, a settings file that is not valid JSON, a symlink that leads out of the repository), the list stays a proposal and the session start says why; `toolprune apply` tries again. **[`docs/PLUGIN.md`](docs/PLUGIN.md)** records how each agent's hooks and settings were verified to behave, and **[`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)** how the package fits together. ### When a turn gets stuck The loop guard first learns how long a turn in this repository usually runs: it waits until *e* turns here have ended well, on their own and with no failing check after the last edit. After that, a turn that shows signs of looping (the same failures repeating, or errors piling up) goes to the judge. One case is redirected without the judge: a turn that runs past *b* times the usual length while churning the same edits through the same failures. If a turn is still stuck after its redirects, you see one line that ends with how to stop it: > TokenEconomizer: this turn still looks stuck after a redirect (judge-stuck@0.82, 46 tool > calls). Press Esc to interrupt it. Where that line appears, and how to stop the turn, in the terminal UI and in a headless run (`claude -p`, `codex exec`, `copilot -p`, `pi -p`, `opencode run`, `hermes -z`): | Agent | Interactive: where it shows | How to stop | Headless: where it shows | How to stop | |---|---|---|---|---| | Claude Code | in Claude's reply | Esc | in the final reply | Ctrl+C | | Codex | in the conversation | Esc, then `/stop` | not shown | Ctrl+C | | Copilot CLI | in the conversation | Esc twice | on stdout | Ctrl+C | | Pi | as a notification | Esc | on stderr | Ctrl+C | | opencode | as a notification | Esc | on stderr | Ctrl+C | | Hermes Agent | in the model's reply | Ctrl+C | in the final reply | Ctrl+C | - **Claude Code** shows a plugin's own lines only in its detailed transcript (Ctrl+O), so the plugin asks Claude to repeat this one in its reply; the model may word it differently or leave it out. - **Codex**: Esc interrupts the turn, but a command it started keeps running until `/stop`. `codex exec` prints no hook messages. - **Pi**: Ctrl+C ends a headless run, but a command it started runs on until it finishes. - **opencode** 2.x prints the line to the opencode server's error output, not in its terminal UI. - **Hermes Agent**: the plugin asks the model to repeat the line, since no hook was found to reach the person's view; a model may word it differently or leave it out. In a headless run nobody may be watching, so a flagged turn runs until it ends or reaches the agent's own limits; afterwards, `te status` counts the redirects and "still stuck" notices. ## Repository | | | |---|---| | [`tokeneconomizer/microskills`](tokeneconomizer/microskills/) | Micro-skill synthesis and injection: facts learned from finished sessions | | [`tokeneconomizer/toolprune`](tokeneconomizer/toolprune/) | Tool pruning: unused tools and Codex capability packages | | [`tokeneconomizer/loopguard`](tokeneconomizer/loopguard/) | Failure-loop intervention: the per-call guard and its per-repository envelope | | [`tokeneconomizer/trace`](tokeneconomizer/trace/) | Each agent's session log, read into one shape | | [`tokeneconomizer/plugin`](tokeneconomizer/plugin/) | The runtime the hooks and the `te` command run | | [`plugin`](plugin/) | The installable plugin: manifests, hook files, launchers, slash commands, the Pi extension, the opencode and Hermes plugins | | [`experiments`](experiments/) | The harness, launchers and task sets behind the paper's results | | [`docs`](docs/) | `PLUGIN.md` (design, verified agent behavior) and `ARCHITECTURE.md` (how the package fits together) | | [`tests`](tests/) | Offline tests for the package and the plugin | The package is standard-library only. Run the tests with `python -m pytest tests` (add `experiments/tests` for the benchmark side), and build a self-contained plugin bundle with `python3 scripts/build_plugin.py --out dist/marketplace`. ## Reproducing the experiments The code behind the paper's results -- a harness that runs Claude Code, Codex and the Copilot CLI on SWE-Bench and Web-Bench, the launchers, and the evaluated task sets -- is in **[`experiments/`](experiments/README.md)**, whose README gives the setup and one command per result. It is not part of the installed plugin; the two share only `tokeneconomizer/`. ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{li2026tokeneconomizer, title = {{TokenEconomizer}: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents}, author = {Li, Aaron J. and Xu, Weijia and Singh, Chandan and Chen, Zixiao and Inala, Jeevana Priya and Siska, Charlotte and Tamersoy, Acar and Yu, Bin and Stoica, Ion and Galley, Michel and Gao, Jianfeng}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2610.22732}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.CL}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22732} } ``` ## License Apache 2.0; see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).
